name: Abraham Lincoln
summary: A self-taught Illinois lawyer and Whig turned Republican who held that the Union is perpetual and that no state may lawfully secede, and led the Union through the Civil War. He called slavery morally wrong but at first aimed only to stop its spread, later issued the Emancipation Proclamation and pressed for the Thirteenth Amendment. He backed protective tariffs, federal support for railroads, land grants and a homestead law, and held that labor ranks above capital while capital has rights. In 1858 he rejected social and political equality of the races, and by April 1865 he favored suffrage for some Black men.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Signed the Revenue Act of 1861, the first national income tax, and in 1864 agreed that a larger share of war costs should come from taxation; he did not call for taxes on the wealthy to be 'significantly higher'.

property-fundamental.rationale: Said capital has rights as worthy of protection as any other, and proposed compensated emancipation, but also freed slaves by the war power without compensation and urged emancipation over the property claims of slaveholders.

state-harmful.rationale: Personally mobilized national government to preserve the republic and defended its essential protective role.

empower-police-military.rationale: Expanded Union forces and requested 400,000 men and $400 million to sustain them.

decide-locally.rationale: Assigned matters concerning only a state to that state, while reserving common concerns to national government.

more-religion-public.rationale: Required Christian Sabbath observance in the military and publicly called the nation to religious fasting and repentance.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Issued the Emancipation Proclamation, urged the Thirteenth Amendment and backed limited Black suffrage, but said little of remedying past injustice beyond ending slavery.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Urged transmission of the founders’ republican inheritance, shared patriotic memory and reverence for national institutions.

gradual-change.rationale: Urged reverence for the laws and long preferred gradual, compensated emancipation, but in 1862 said 'the dogmas of the quiet past are inadequate to the stormy present' and acted by war power.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Asked Congress to encourage immigration, called immigrants 'one of the principal replenishing streams' that repair war's losses, and signed an act for the encouragement of immigration.

free-trade.rationale: As president he signed repeated increases to the protective Morrill Tariff rather than lowering duties; he did not argue the free-trade case in the sources read.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

revolution-justified.rationale: Said that when the people grow weary of the government they have a constitutional right of amending it or a 'revolutionary right to dismember or overthrow it', while denying that secession by a state was lawful.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Signed increases to the Morrill Tariff, which raised import duties considerably and were designed in part to help manufacturers offset the burden of new taxes.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Signed the Pacific Railroad Act of 1862 to back construction of the transcontinental railroad with federal support, and urged Congress to fund a railroad to loyal east Tennessee as a strategic measure.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Praised the system in which a penniless beginner saves wages to buy tools or land and works on his own account, and with families working their own farms; signed the 1862 Homestead Act opening public land to small settlers.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Called the system in which a beginner labors for wages, saves, and later hires others 'the just and generous and prosperous system'; the Emancipation Proclamation urged freed people to labor for reasonable wages.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Championed federally supervised currency and national banking, opposing money left entirely to the market; this predates modern central banks.

one-party-rule.rationale: Maintained a contested presidential election during civil war, although he also suppressed some antiwar activity.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In his workingmen’s reply, opposed monarchy as a retreat from popular institutions into despotism.

democracy-best.rationale: Called a majority held by constitutional limits 'the only true sovereign of a free people' and the war a test whether government of the people can keep its territorial integrity; ended at Gettysburg on government of the people, by the people, for the people.

right-to-secede.rationale: Held that no State upon its own mere motion can lawfully get out of the Union, called secession 'the essence of anarchy' and its legal basis a sophism.

natural-rulers.rationale: Inferred: from his statement that no man is good enough to govern another without that other's consent.

political-violence-never.rationale: Condemned mob violence in 1838 and said elections should settle disputes, but led a war to put down rebellion and acknowledged the people's revolutionary right; ambiguous for 'political violence'.

separate-church-state.rationale: Explicitly rejected government control of churches and appointment of their ministers, while supporting public religious observance.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Described the Union's aim as clearing the path for all and affording 'all an unfettered start and a fair chance in the race of life', that is equal opportunity, and said men should enjoy what they honestly earn.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: His administration's Native American policy focused on assimilation and diminishing tribal landholdings, while it opened western lands to settlers by the Homestead Act and Pacific railroad grants.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Presented inventions, printing and industrial arts as major advances in humanity’s material and intellectual condition.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Said what he did about slavery he did to save the Union, that he would do less or more as it helped the cause, and that he would 'adopt new views so fast as they shall appear to be true views'.

direct-action.rationale: Argued that ballots, rather than a resort to bullets after electoral defeat, are the proper avenue for political change.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Described free laborers 'taking the whole product to themselves' and said men should not touch what they have not honestly earned, which ties reward to work, not need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Held that capital is the fruit of labor and labor deserves higher consideration, but that capital 'has its rights' and that hiring free labor is a mutually beneficial, just relation, not a fixed class exploitation.

collective-farming.rationale: Inferred: he praised families working their own farms and taking the whole product to themselves, which points against collective farming; he never addressed collective farms.

taxation-theft.rationale: Called for additional taxation to finance the war as a legitimate national obligation.

conscription.rationale: His 1863 message treats drafting into military service as operating law and, in 1863, he defended the death penalty for desertion as necessary to maintain armies.

hereditarian-race.rationale: In 1858 conceded Black Americans were not equal to whites 'perhaps' in moral or intellectual endowment and that a physical difference forbids living together as equals; tentative, and he later made no such claim.

territorial-expansion.rationale: As a congressman in 1847 pressed the 'spot resolutions' challenging President Polk's account of the start of the Mexican war; no statement favoring expansion by force.

bound-labor.rationale: Inferred: he opposed forcing people to labor without their consent, calling slavery wrong and saying a free man is not fixed for life in one condition of labor; he did not address land-bound labor owed to a lord as such.

universal-morality.rationale: Held that slavery's wrong is a moral truth ('If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong'), and that the Declaration's self-evident truths apply to all men.

national-self-determination.rationale: Endorsed sufficiently numerous peoples choosing their government in the Hungarian resolutions; distinguished this from unilateral state secession.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Urged in 1838 that 'cold, calculating, unimpassioned reason' must govern and in 1842 praised 'all conquering mind', but he also spoke in providential terms in later years.

class-collaboration.rationale: Said there is and probably always will be a relation between labor and capital 'producing mutual benefits' and denied that hired laborers are fixed in a class for life, while ranking labor above capital.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: In 1865 approved Louisiana’s equal public schooling for Black and white children; this is limited evidence, not comprehensive racial equality.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Supported public promotion of mineral exploration, immigration and strategic infrastructure beyond defense, justice and property protection.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: In 1858 said he was not in favor of black and white people intermarrying and pledged to stand by the Illinois law forbidding it; he made no later statement.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Held that Black Americans are entitled to the Declaration's rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness and are 'equal' to any man in the right to eat the bread their own hands earn; in 1858 he denied favoring voting, jury service or social equality, and in 1865 favored suffrage only for the very intelligent and soldiers.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Said 'no man is good enough to govern another man, without that other's consent' and called this the 'sheet anchor of American republicanism'.

population-transfer.rationale: Supported colonization of freed Black Americans abroad but only as voluntary emigration, saying no one should be forced; by 1864 he no longer urged it. Not aimed at a minority seen as hostile.

separated-powers.rationale: Stressed constitutional checks and limitations on majority power and worked with Congress, but exercised broad executive war powers, drawing Chief Justice Taney's objection in Ex parte Merryman.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Suspended the writ of habeas corpus in 1861 and defended arrests without ordinary process as constitutional measures indispensable to public safety against rebellion and its sympathizers.

party-controls-media.rationale: Ordered military seizure and closure of two New York newspapers over a forged proclamation in May 1864.

head-commands-forces.rationale: As president he supervised Union strategy and the selection of generals as commander-in-chief and chose his cabinet.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Explicitly denied that farmers are morally better or worse than members of other occupations.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Ranked societies by their development in arts and inventions and contrasted progressive civilization with stagnation.

death-penalty.rationale: Upheld executions of 38 Dakota men after pardoning most of 303 condemned and said the severe penalty of death for desertion is sanctioned by law; no statement on terrorism as such.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Personally sought release of Quaker objectors, as Pringle’s diary reports; his later promise of assistance remained qualified by law.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Insisted that churches manage their own affairs and that government must not control either religious faction.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Held that no state can lawfully leave the Union and used the war power to resist force employed against the Union.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Told Congress it should not be that one sworn to execute the laws faithfully should himself violate them and in 1838 urged all to reverence the laws; he also argued measures 'otherwise unconstitutional' could become lawful when indispensable to preserve the nation.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Called majority rule legitimate when 'held in restraint by constitutional checks and limitations' and said rule by a minority as a permanent arrangement is inadmissible.

patriotic-education.rationale: Called for schools and colleges to cultivate national constitutional loyalty and reverence for the founders’ legacy.

public-money-creation.rationale: Signed the Legal Tender Act creating Treasury greenbacks, called them a universal currency that met a long-felt want, but also backed the 1863 National Banking Act, under which private national banks issued notes against federal bonds.

elective-rulers.rationale: Declared regular elections indispensable to free government and personally submitted to reelection.

minority-veto.rationale: Rejected unanimity and a dissenting minority’s permanent control over a constitutional majority.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: In his Second Inaugural, identified slavery as the interest underlying the war.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Required obedience even to bad laws until their repeal, expressly rejecting private disregard of them.

non-intervention.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

religious-nation.rationale: Countermanded collective expulsion of Jews and reportedly denied religious distinctions among citizens, despite Christian public rhetoric.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Praised wage work leading to private ownership and hiring as a system producing prosperity, opportunity and improvement.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Defended military restraint of antiwar agitation deemed harmful to recruitment, despite accepting ordinary political opposition.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Located presidential authority entirely in the people and political sovereignty in a constitutionally constrained popular majority.

racial-franchise.rationale: By April 1865 favored votes for intelligent Black men and Black veterans, reversing his earlier blanket exclusion.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Praised small independent producers as free from domination by money and land magnates.

abolish-ip.rationale: Praised time-limited patent exclusivity for giving inventors a material incentive to innovate.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Explicitly endorsed the platform’s permanent national gratitude and everlasting remembrance for those killed defending the country.

sacred-nation.rationale: Presented the republic as an intergenerational inheritance demanding sacred pledges and continuing collective sacrifice.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

women-suffrage.rationale: His 1836 suffrage proposal expressly included white women, with tax-or-arms qualifications; historians dispute whether the remark was serious.

self-ownership.rationale: In his April 1864 Baltimore address, distinguished liberty over oneself and one’s labor from mastery over others.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Explicitly said bad laws should be obeyed until repealed, rejecting their injustice as sufficient to disregard them.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Presented defense of the Union as defense of working people’s political rights and opportunities.

notes:
Views changed: he favored voluntary colonization of freed Black Americans in 1854 and 1862 but dropped it by 1864; he said in 1858 he did not favor Black voting or jury service, and on 11 April 1865 said he would prefer the franchise for the very intelligent and for soldiers. The later position is used where a statement touches these. Answers marked 'Inferred:' are low confidence. Racial-segregation and colonization statements were answered only where his words match the wording: his support for separation was by emigration, not segregation law inside the country, so racial-segregation-law is null.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 41 answers taken from it, 28 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass; the previous audit was consulted only for metadata, sources, notes and the authorized null list. Full active list and remaining nulls reviewed. Rhetoric is at most medium. The Hungarian resolutions are joint committee resolutions presented by Lincoln, not proof of exclusive authorship; their intervention exception is distinguished from his later practical neutrality. No position on great-power blocs, ending permanent alliances or multipolarity was found. Providence and collective repentance do not establish scriptural civil law or divine rather than popular political authority. Spiritual interpretations of the war do not establish a fundamental good-versus-evil political dualism. Gettysburg and other renewal language are insufficient for radical national rebirth after decadence. Lyceum civil religion supports a qualified sacred national community, not a religious test of national membership, ancient uninterrupted identity, or environmental stewardship. Small private farms are not cooperative common-property communities. Patent incentives and technological optimism do not establish that technology solves most human problems. Capital-created-by-labor is not a goods-value theory. Church autonomy coexists with Christian military observance; neither establishes his view of religious instruction in state schools. Gurney supports qualified conscience relief, not immunity from every general law. The 1864 platform is used because he personally endorsed it on June 27, with an express Mexico qualification. His final Black-suffrage proposal supersedes blanket exclusion in 1858; Louisiana equal schooling is narrower than comprehensive racial equality and does not retract his marriage position. His voluntary overseas colonization advocacy and pressure on Black leaders in 1862 were not a plan to deport all freed people; historians dispute when or whether he fully abandoned the policy, and the late Butler account is contested. This is not silently treated as a settled 1864 repudiation. Internal tribal removal and Grant’s departmental expulsion of Jews are not by themselves expulsion from the country of a minority seen as hostile; population-transfer remains null. The personal pledge supporting tribal removal is distinguished from formal assent alone. Modern nuclear, internet, climate and algorithmic positions remain unknown. Only rationales beginning Inferred: are historical inferences.
